claims.text: Chemical short-range order suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys relative to a random solid solution.
The additional suppression arises from phonon scattering by antiphase boundaries and local lattice-strain variations.
SRO-induced suppression applies when the SRO correlation length is shorter than the phonon mean free path.
A random MoNbTaW-like refractory alloy has high compositional disorder and severe lattice distortion.
The baseline lattice thermal conductivity of the random alloy is dominated by point-defect scattering.
An equilibrium SRO state of MoNbTaW can be produced or represented at 800 K.
Thermal annealing at 800 K can induce SRO in MoNbTaW without causing long-range phase separation.
The proposed refractory alloy may form L12- or L11-type SRO domains.
Phonons are the dominant heat carriers in the refractory alloy from 300 K to 2000 K.
SRO domains have characteristic sizes of approximately 0.9–1.2 nm in a related alloy system.
SRO in MoNbTaW is associated with diffuse antiphase boundaries.
Interfaces of SRO domains generate local lattice-strain fields.
SRO can enhance edge-dislocation mobility in MoNbTaW.
DAPBs and static chemical-ordering variations scatter phonons whose wavelengths are comparable to the roughly 1 nm SRO-domain size.
SRO-induced scattering reduces the phonon mean free path relative to scattering from mass variance and size mismatch in the random state.
The reduction in lattice thermal conductivity should be greatest at intermediate temperatures before phonon-phonon scattering becomes dominant.
The magnitude of lattice-thermal-conductivity suppression increases with the SRO parameter and DAPB density.
Rapid quenching from a high-temperature disordered state yields a fully randomized solid solution suitable as the baseline.
The suppression regime requires nanoscale SRO below 2 nm and a single-phase alloy.
The SRO-induced suppression diminishes or vanishes when SRO develops into long-range ordered precipitates or is randomized above 2000 K.
